growthlab.name: GrowthLab
growthlab.title: Turn generic outreach into relevant sales conversations.
growthlab.description: Four-email cold outreach sequence built around curiosity, specific observations and a low-friction question.
growthlab.email:
Hi [First Name],
[Specific observation about their business or target market] caught my eye.
It gave me an idea for how [Company] could approach [buyer type]: lead with [specific buyer problem], then connect it
to your offer.
At GrowthLab, we help B2B teams build outreach around the buyer’s situation, so there’s a clear reason to reply.
Want me to send over the opening email I have in mind?
[Sender Name]
GrowthLab
growthlab.fulltext:
ABDUL TAHIR GrowthLab / BRIEF & STRATEGY                                                             1 / 3


CLIENT PROJECT | B2B AGENCY · LEAD GENERATION
Turn generic outreach into relevant
sales conversations.
A four-email cold sequence for GrowthLab, a B2B agency, written to earn a reply before asking
for a meeting.
PROJECT 1 | MARCH 2025 | COPYWRITER: ABDUL TAHIR

 Natural tone   Short structure    Curiosity-led hook


AUDIENCE           Decision-makers at B2B companies who are working on their outbound.

THE BRIEF          GrowthLab's outreach was being opened but not answered. The emails read like
                    templates, so prospects had no particular reason to reply.

GOAL               Increase reply rates by replacing generic outreach with conversational copy.

MY APPROACH             I rewrote the sequence in a natural tone, with short paragraphs and one question per
                     email. The first email doesn't ask for a meeting. It offers an idea and lets the prospect
                   decide whether to see it.

DELIVERABLES     A four-email sequence with send timing (Days 1, 4, 8 and 13) and fields for
                     personalisation.

How the sequence builds

 01    Start with an observation          Email 1 opens with something specific about the prospect's business or market, which gives the
         message a reason to exist.

 02    Offer something useful first          Email 2 shares the angle itself. The prospect gets an idea to react to before anyone asks for their
            time.

 03    Get the targeting right          Email 3 raises the buyer segment. Who receives the email matters as much as what it says.





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR GrowthLab / EMAIL SEQUENCE                                                              2 / 3

The sequence
Four emails over 13 days. Emails 2 to 4 continue in the same thread.

  01 / EMAIL 1 • DAY 1
   Start the conversation
   Hi [First Name],
   [Specific observation about their business or target market] caught my eye.
    It gave me an idea for how [Company] could approach [buyer type]: lead with [specific buyer problem], then connect it
   to your offer.
   At GrowthLab, we help B2B teams build outreach around the buyer’s situation, so there’s a clear reason to reply.
  Want me to send over the opening email I have in mind?
  [Sender Name]
  GrowthLab

  02 / EMAIL 2 • DAY 4
   Give them something useful | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
   Here’s the angle I mentioned:
  “[One sentence connecting a verified observation to a problem your prospect can solve.]”
  That gives the buyer something specific to respond to before you ask for their time.
  For [Company], I’d build the follow-ups around the same problem, with a different reason to reply in each one.
  Would a short sequence outline be useful?
  [Sender Name]
  GrowthLab

  03 / EMAIL 3 • DAY 8
  Address the targeting problem | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
  One other thought: who receives the email matters as much as what it says.
  For [Company], I’d start with [specific buyer segment] because [verified reason the offer is relevant to them].
  A smaller, focused campaign would give your team a clearer view of which message gets a response.
   Is that a segment you’re already approaching?
  [Sender Name]
  GrowthLab

  04 / EMAIL 4 • DAY 13
   Close without pressure | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
     I’ll leave this here after today.
    If improving outbound is on your list, I can send the email outline for [Company] for you to review. No meeting needed.
    If the timing isn’t right, no problem.
  Should I send it over?
  [Sender Name]
  GrowthLab





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR GrowthLab / RATIONALE                                                                    3 / 3

Copy decisions

TONE                Plain wording, as if one person were writing to another. Nothing in it reads like an
                 agency brochure.

STRUCTURE          Short paragraphs and a single question at the end of each email, so the next step is
                  easy to answer.

THE HOOK         The first email leads with an idea (“the opening email I have in mind”) rather than a
                    request for time.

PERSONALISATION    Bracketed fields such as [Company] and [Specific observation] are filled for each
                    prospect, using a detail that can be verified.

THE ENDING        The last email offers the outline with no meeting attached, and makes it easy to say
                    no.

Sequence at a glance

 DAY     EMAIL                   WHAT IT DOES

 Day 1     Start the conversation          Opens with an observation and offers to send the opening email.

 Day 4    Give them something useful       Shares the angle and offers a short sequence outline.

 Day 8    Address the targeting problem     Asks whether the suggested buyer segment is already being
                                           approached.

 Day 13   Close without pressure             Offers the outline, no meeting needed.

talentbridge.fulltext:
ABDUL TAHIR TalentBridge / BRIEF & STRATEGY                                                           1 / 3


CLIENT PROJECT | RECRUITING FIRM · CANDIDATE OUTREACH
Replace the template with a real
question.
A four-email cold sequence for TalentBridge, a recruiting firm, built around one question about
candidate replies.
PROJECT 2 | APRIL 2025 | COPYWRITER: ABDUL TAHIR

 Observational opening    Conversational tone    Soft CTA


AUDIENCE            Recruiting and hiring leads who send candidate outreach.

THE BRIEF            Recruiting emails tend to sound alike, and candidates notice. Generic outreach
                     signals low effort, so it blends into the rest of the inbox and goes unanswered.

GOAL              Improve candidate reply rates by replacing templated recruiting outreach with copy
                      that feels personal and human.

MY APPROACH             I opened with a plain question about reply rates instead of an introduction. The
                     follow-ups explain what makes a message feel written for one person, show an
                 example opening, and close with an easy way out.

DELIVERABLES     A four-email sequence with a subject line and a soft, reply-based call to action.

What shapes the copy

 01    Observational opening          Email 1 starts from something the reader can check for themselves: whether their candidates are
            replying right now.

 02    Conversational tone        A lowercase subject line, a first-name greeting and short lines. It reads like a note from a person, not
         a campaign.

 03    Soft CTA          Every email ends by offering something small, a short note or an example. None of them asks for a
              call.





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR TalentBridge / EMAIL SEQUENCE                                                            2 / 3

The sequence
Four emails over 13 days. Emails 2 to 4 continue in the same thread.

  01 / EMAIL 1 • DAY 1
   Start with the question
  Subject: quick question about candidate replies
   Hi [First Name],
  Quick question: are your candidates actually replying to outreach right now?
    I ask because [specific observation about their open roles or hiring activity]. I'm with TalentBridge, where we recruit for
   [roles or sector].
    If replies have been slow, I can send a short note on how we write the first message to a candidate. No call needed.
  Would that be useful?
  [Sender Name]
   TalentBridge

  02 / EMAIL 2 • DAY 4
   Explain what makes a message specific | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
  Candidates can usually tell within a line or two whether a message was written for them or for a list.
  What helps is a specific reason for the contact: a project they've worked on, a skill the role needs, or a detail about the
  team.
   That's the part I'd focus on for [role]. Is that how your outreach opens today?
  [Sender Name]
   TalentBridge

  03 / EMAIL 3 • DAY 8
  Show an example opening | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
   Here's the kind of opening I mean:
  “[One line about a verified detail in the candidate's work, followed by why the role fits.]”
    It's short, plain and easy to answer. I can draft one for [role] so you can compare it with your current message.
  Want me to send it over?
  [Sender Name]
   TalentBridge

  04 / EMAIL 4 • DAY 13
   Close politely | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
     I'll leave this with you.
    If candidate replies are on your list, reply and I'll send the example for [role]. If your outreach is already working well,
   there's nothing to change.
   All the best,
  [Sender Name]
   TalentBridge





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR TalentBridge / RATIONALE                                                                  3 / 3

Copy decisions

WHY A QUESTION    A question the reader can answer in one line is easier to reply to than a pitch.

NO PITCH UP FRONT   The first email asks before it tells, which earns the right to say more in the follow-ups.

AN EXAMPLE, NOT A   Email 3 shows the kind of opening line it means, so the reader can judge the
PROMISE                  approach for themselves.

A RESPECTFUL      The final email accepts that the reader's outreach may already be working, which
CLOSE                  keeps the tone courteous.

Sequence at a glance

 DAY     EMAIL                   WHAT IT DOES

 Day 1     Start with the question           Asks whether candidates are replying and offers a short note.

 Day 4     Explain what makes a message    Describes the specific reason for contact that candidates respond to.
              specific

 Day 8    Show an example opening         Offers to draft an opening line for a named role.

 Day 13   Close politely                  Leaves the offer open and accepts that nothing may need to change.

invoiceflow.fulltext:
ABDUL TAHIR InvoiceFlow / BRIEF & STRATEGY                                                            1 / 3


CLIENT PROJECT | B2B SOFTWARE · LEAD GENERATION
Reduce the effort of keeping track of
unpaid invoices.
A four-email cold sequence for InvoiceFlow, a B2B invoicing software company, written to turn
cold prospects into booked demos.
PROJECT 3 | JULY 2025 | COPYWRITER: ABDUL TAHIR

 Conversational copy    Curiosity-led hook   Demo-focused journey


AUDIENCE         Teams that send invoices and follow up on late payments.

THE BRIEF           InvoiceFlow had a strong product, but its outreach explained it through features. The
                   emails listed what the software does and gave a finance or operations reader little to
                   recognise from their own week.

GOAL              Convert cold prospects into booked demos through conversational, curiosity-driven
                    copy.

MY APPROACH             I built the sequence around one task: following up on an overdue invoice. The emails
                  ask how the team handles it today, describe the checks involved, and then offer a
               demo that follows a single invoice from start to finish.

DELIVERABLES     A four-email sequence with a focused demo invitation and a polite final email.

How the sequence builds

 01   Lead with a familiar problem          Email 1 asks how the team keeps track of what's paid, what's overdue and who needs a reminder.

 02   Make the pain tangible          Email 2 uses three short questions (Did someone send a reminder? Did the client reply? Who has
           the next step?) to describe the confusion of chasing a payment.

 03    Give the demo a clear scope          Email 3 narrows the walkthrough to one example, an overdue invoice, so the reader knows what
           they would be agreeing to.





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR InvoiceFlow / EMAIL SEQUENCE                                                             2 / 3

The sequence
Four emails over 13 days. Emails 2 to 4 continue in the same thread.

  01 / EMAIL 1 • DAY 1
  Lead with a familiar problem
   Hi [First Name],
  Once an invoice goes out at [Company], how does your team keep track of what’s paid, what’s overdue, and who
  needs a reminder?
   InvoiceFlow helps bring invoice tracking and payment follow-ups into one workflow, so your team can spend less time
  checking spreadsheets and email threads.
  Would a quick look at that workflow be useful?
  [Sender Name]
   InvoiceFlow

  02 / EMAIL 2 • DAY 4
  Make the pain tangible | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
  The awkward part of chasing an invoice is often figuring out what’s already happened.
  Did someone send a reminder? Did the client reply? Who’s handling the next step?
   That’s the workflow I’d focus on in an InvoiceFlow demo: checking the invoice status and seeing what needs attention
   next.
   Is that something your team currently handles manually?
  [Sender Name]
   InvoiceFlow

  03 / EMAIL 3 • DAY 8
  Make the demo specific | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
    If you’re open to a demo, we can keep it focused on one example: an invoice that’s overdue.
  We’d walk through how your team would find it, review its status, and handle the follow-up in InvoiceFlow.
  That should give you a practical sense of whether it fits your process.
  Would you be open to taking a look next week?
  [Sender Name]
   InvoiceFlow

  04 / EMAIL 4 • DAY 13
   Give an easy exit | Same email thread
   Hi [First Name],
     I’ll wrap up here.
    If your current invoicing process works well, fair enough.
    If tracking unpaid invoices and coordinating reminders still takes more time than you’d like, we can show you how
   InvoiceFlow handles that workflow.
  Worth revisiting, or should I leave it here?
  [Sender Name]
   InvoiceFlow





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR InvoiceFlow / RATIONALE                                                                   3 / 3

Copy decisions

ONE WORKFLOW, NOT Every email returns to the same task. The product appears as the place where that
A FEATURE LIST                    task happens.

QUESTIONS BEFORE  The early emails ask what the reader's process looks like instead of telling them what
CLAIMS                          is wrong with it.

A SMALL, SPECIFIC   A demo built around one invoice sounds shorter and easier to agree to than a general
ASK                    product tour.

AN EASY EXIT       The last email accepts that the current process may already work well, and leaves the
                    decision with the reader.

Sequence at a glance

 DAY     EMAIL                   WHAT IT DOES

 Day 1    Lead with a familiar problem      Asks how the team tracks paid, overdue and reminder-needed
                                                  invoices.

 Day 4    Make the pain tangible            Describes the confusion of chasing an invoice and the workflow a
                                   demo would cover.

 Day 8    Make the demo specific            Offers a focused demo around one overdue invoice.

 Day 13   Give an easy exit                Closes politely and asks whether to revisit or leave it.

scaleops.fulltext:
ABDUL TAHIR ScaleOps / BRIEF & STRATEGY                                                              1 / 3


CLIENT PROJECT | B2B SAAS · SIGNAL-BASED PROSPECTING
One growth signal. One short email.
A plain-text outreach email for ScaleOps, a B2B SaaS company, sent only when a prospect
shows a specific growth signal.
PROJECT 4 | AUGUST 2026 | COPYWRITER: ABDUL TAHIR

 Trigger-based targeting   Short plain text    Low-friction CTA


AUDIENCE           VP-level sales leaders at companies showing a growth signal, such as hiring a new
             SDR team.

THE BRIEF          ScaleOps was sending long, five-paragraph emails built on HTML-heavy templates
                     with tracking links. VP-level prospects were tuning them out, and deliverability was
                       suffering.

GOAL            Keep the emails out of spam and give VP-level prospects a reason to reply.

MY APPROACH             I cut the email back to a few lines of plain text, with no links or images, and tied each
                 send to a real trigger. The email goes out only when the prospect shows a growth
                       signal, so the first line explains why it arrived.

DELIVERABLES     A signal-triggered, plain-text outreach email.

Three changes

 01    Trigger-based targeting         The email is sent only when a target company shows a specific growth signal, for example hiring a
        new SDR team.

 02    Short plain text         Around 40 words, no formatting, written to be read on a phone in a few seconds.

 03   No links or images         Removing them reduces spam-filter risk and helps protect inbox placement.





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR ScaleOps / EMAIL SEQUENCE                                                               2 / 3

Email sample
Plain text, no links, no images.

  EMAIL SAMPLE
   Triggered by an SDR hiring signal
  Subject: SDR hiring
   Hi [First Name],
  Saw you just brought on 4 new SDRs this week. Nice work.
   Usually, scaling that fast breaks lead routing—reps end up wasting hours doing it manually.
  We built a lightweight backend tool at ScaleOps to fix that exact bottleneck.
  Worth a look?

Reading the email

SUBJECT LINE      “SDR hiring” names the signal, so the reader sees the reason for the email straight
                  away.

OPENING LINE       Acknowledges the growth signal with a short congratulation instead of a generic
                   compliment.

MIDDLE LINE       Names the problem that often follows fast hiring: lead routing.

CLOSING LINE       Connects ScaleOps to that one bottleneck, with no feature list.

CTA            A three-word question that asks for a look, not a call, so replying takes almost no
                          effort.





Abdul Tahir  | B2B Email Copywriter | Ghostwriter

ABDUL TAHIR ScaleOps / RATIONALE                                                                     3 / 3

Copy decisions

SIGNAL BEFORE     The hiring signal explains the timing and gives a VP a reason to read past the first
PITCH                          line.

ONE PROBLEM ONLY  The email names a single bottleneck instead of describing the product.

WRITTEN FOR MOBILE The whole message fits on one phone screen without scrolling.

PLAIN TEXT, NO LINKS  It avoids the HTML formatting and tracking links that were hurting the client's
                        deliverability.

A SMALL ASK       The closing question is easy to answer and doesn't commit the reader to anything.
